title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What does the module identify as the more revealing half of the AI-policy statistics? `[V]`
options: That 51% of organizations have no formal AI use policy

That among organizations which do have one, 54% say it is too tied to today's specific tools and 23% say it is too broad — so roughly three in four that did the work think the artifact doesn't function
That policies are usually written by legal rather than HR
That employees are largely unaware their organization has a policy
questions.explanation: The 51% is a compliance gap. The 54%/23% split is a design failure, and it repeats because everyone makes the same mistake — naming products, which gives a policy a shelf life equal to the vendor's release cadence.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a policy and an enablement decision?
options: A policy is mandatory; an enablement decision is advisory
A policy is written by HR; an enablement decision is written by IT
A policy governs people and succeeds if they can comply without asking anyone; an enablement decision governs a system and succeeds if it explains a choice somebody made to an auditor
They are the same document at different levels of detail
questions.explanation: Most organizations wrote the first and believe it covers the second. The missing document is the one this role owns, and Module 7 asks for its signature.

questions.prompt: Which of the eight questions does the module say uncovers the most real problems?
options: What population does it reach
What does it write versus read
What happens when it is wrong at 3am on a Saturday — because the answer is usually a named person who lacks the access they would need
Who is accountable by name
questions.explanation: The others surface design gaps. This one surfaces the gap between the named responder and their actual permissions, which only appears when you check.

questions.prompt: Why is "with human oversight" not an answer to the human-gate question?
options: Because oversight must be documented in the contract

Because it names no person, no step, and says nothing about whether that person has the authority or the time to refuse — a gate staffed by someone with 400 items a day and no mandate to reject is not a gate
Because human oversight is prohibited under the EU AI Act
Because oversight should be automated for consistency
questions.explanation: It is a reassurance shaped like an answer. The test is whether refusal is actually available to the named person.

questions.prompt: Why does the autonomy ladder from 201 M5 need rethinking for a vendor-built capability?
options: Because vendor capabilities are always more autonomous than self-built ones
Because the ladder still describes the risk exactly, but you control none of its rungs — what autonomy, evidence and stopping power you have are contractual facts fixed at signature
Because the ladder only applies to workflows involving employee data
Because vendors implement the middle rung by default
questions.explanation: Which turns an engineering question into a procurement one, and your leverage exists exactly once — before you sign. Afterwards you have a renewal in eighteen months and an obligation today.

questions.prompt: How should the *Kistler v. Eightfold* litigation be characterized? `[V]`
options: A ruling establishing that AI hiring tools are consumer reporting agencies under FCRA
A settled case that changed employer obligations for candidate data
A pending complaint in the pleading stage with no ruling on a motion to dismiss — a live question rather than a holding
Irrelevant to People Operations, since it concerns recruiting tools
questions.explanation: Carry the posture accurately; anyone saying the law has changed is ahead of the record. And D is wrong for a specific reason: the questions it raises — where data came from, whether the subject was told, whether a dispute path exists — are data-flow and workflow questions, which are this role's artifacts.

questions.prompt: What is the transferable provenance question the module extracts?
options: Whether the vendor has a SOC 2 report covering its data sources

Whether the capability's output depends on data its subject has never seen — because a disclosure-and-dispute path will eventually be demanded, and retrofitting one across a live integration is a project
Whether third-party data is stored inside your tenancy
Whether the data was obtained with consent from the original platform
questions.explanation: It applies to every AI feature in the stack, not only candidate-facing ones. Asking before enablement costs one line in a review.

questions.prompt: Why does the module say sandbox testing rarely answers the real question?
options: Because sandbox environments run older software versions
Because sandboxes have synthetic data, no integration traffic and no real users — while the failures that matter are integration failures and human failures
Because sandbox results cannot be included in an audit trail
Because vendors restrict AI features in non-production environments
questions.explanation: Sandbox proves the feature exists and functions. Use it for the rollback rehearsal, then pilot in production on a scoped population — which is only possible if the capability can be scoped, which is why that is question one.
